title: Isidore of Seville
hookLine: he tried to gather all human knowledge into one book

cards: What is a star? Why is a horse called a horse? What does a doctor do, what is a city, and how do you build a ship?
One man in Spain set out to answer questions like these, and many more, in a single work. He wasn't a professor in a quiet library. He was a busy bishop in Seville, holding councils, teaching clergy.
And still he kept writing, gathering what earlier writers knew about grammar, law, medicine, animals, stones, the stars and God, so it could sit on one shelf. Today, Isidore of Seville.

teach.h: A BOOK OF NAMES AND THINGS.
teach.b: His big work is called the Etymologies, and the title gives away his method: understand where a thing's name comes from, and you'll understand the thing faster. So he goes word by word.
Here is the name, here is where it comes from, here is what it means.
From there he opens out into everything: how to write, how to argue, how the body works, which trees grow where, what the Church's feasts mean. Isidore didn't claim to invent any of this.
He collected it, reading the older writers, pagan and Christian, and pulling their work together so that what lay scattered could be found in one place. Not all of it holds up.
Some of his word origins are guesses, and readers today smile at them. That doesn't take away what he was doing: keeping a whole world of learning within reach of one reader.
One line from another of his books still gets passed around.
Isidore wrote, roughly, that when we pray, we speak to God, and when we read, God speaks to us. For him, reading was never just collecting facts. It was half of a conversation.
Catholics honor him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. His ambition was all knowledge.
Not because one book could ever hold it, but because learning belonged inside a life turned toward God.

how: The Catholic Church keeps the feast of Saint Isidore of Seville and honors him as a Doctor of the Church; his Etymologies is still read by people who study how learning was kept and passed on.

practice: Pick an ordinary thing near you, a plant, a cup, the weather outside, your own breath, and look at it slowly, the way Isidore looked at a word. What is it made of, where did it come from, who made it or grew it?
Let one question stay with you to look up later, and if you pray, thank God for one thing you'll understand a little better today.

orig.note: Latin, from Greek: an account of where a word comes from. Isidore's book takes its name from it.
